{{Short description|Parameters describing a planet's rigidity}}
{{technical|date=June 2024}}
The '''Love numbers''' ('''''h''''', '''''k''''', and '''''l''''') are [[dimensionless quantity|dimensionless]] parameters that measure the [[stiffness|rigidity]] of a [[planet|planetary body]] or other gravitating object, and the susceptibility of its shape to change in response to an external [[tidal force|tidal potential]].

In 1909, [[Augustus Edward Hough Love]] introduced the values ''h'' and ''k'' which characterize the overall [[elasticity (physics)|elastic]] response of the Earth to the tides—''[[Earth tide]]s'' or ''body tides''.<ref>Love Augustus Edward Hough. The yielding of the earth to disturbing forces 82 Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 1909 http://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1909.0008</ref> Later, in 1912, Toshi Shida added a third Love number, ''l'', which was needed to obtain a complete overall description of the solid Earth's response to the [[tide]]s.<ref>TOSHI SHIDA, On the Body Tides of the Earth, A Proposal for the International Geodetic Association, Proceedings of the Tokyo Mathematico-Physical Society. 2nd Series, 1911-1912, Volume 6, Issue 16, Pages 242-258, ISSN 2185-2693, {{doi|10.11429/ptmps1907.6.16_242}}.</ref>

==Definitions==
The Love number '''''h''''' is defined as the ratio of the body tide to the height of the static [[equilibrium tide]];<ref name="Poulsen">"Tidal Deformation of the Solid Earth: A Finite Difference Discretization", S.K.Poulsen; Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen; p&nbsp;24; [http://cct.gfy.ku.dk/thesis/thesis_stinekp.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011123826/http://cct.gfy.ku.dk/thesis/thesis_stinekp.pdf|date=2016-10-11}}</ref> also defined as the vertical (radial) displacement or variation of the planet's elastic properties. In terms of the tide generating potential <math>V(\theta, \phi )/g</math>, the displacement is <math>h V(\theta, \phi)/g</math> where <math>\theta</math> is latitude, <math>\phi</math> is east longitude and <math>g</math> is acceleration due to gravity.<ref name=EarthTides>Earth Tides; D.C.Agnew, University of California; 2007; 174</ref> For a hypothetical solid Earth <math>h = 0</math>. For a liquid Earth, one would expect <math>h = 1</math>. However, the deformation of the sphere causes the potential field to change, and thereby deform the sphere even more. The theoretical maximum is <math>h = 2.5</math>. For the real Earth, <math>h</math> lies between 0 and 1.

The Love number '''''k''''' is defined as the cubical dilation or the ratio of the additional potential (self-reactive force) produced by the deformation of the deforming potential. It can be represented as <math>k V(\theta, \phi)/g</math>, where <math>k = 0</math> for a rigid body.<ref name=EarthTides/>

The Love number '''''l''''' represents the ratio of the horizontal (transverse) displacement of an element of mass of the planet's crust to that of the corresponding static ocean tide.<ref name=Poulsen/> In potential notation the transverse displacement is <math>l \nabla (V(\theta, \phi))/g</math>, where <math>\nabla</math> is the horizontal [[gradient]] operator. As with ''h'' and ''k'', <math>l = 0</math> for a rigid body.<ref name=EarthTides/>

==Values==
According to Cartwright, "An elastic solid spheroid will yield to an external tide potential <math>U_2</math> of [[spherical harmonic]] degree 2 by a surface tide <math>h_2U_2/g</math> and the self-attraction of this tide will increase the external potential by <math>k_2U_2</math>."<ref name=Cartwright>Tides: A Scientific History; David E. Cartwright; Cambridge University Press, 1999, {{ISBN|0-521-62145-3}}; pp&nbsp;140–141,224</ref> The magnitudes of the Love numbers depend on the rigidity and mass distribution of the spheroid. Love numbers <math>h_n</math>, <math>k_n</math>, and <math>l_n</math> can also be calculated for higher orders of spherical harmonics.

For elastic Earth the Love numbers lie in the range: <math>0.616 \leq h_2 \leq 0.624</math>, <math>0.304 \leq k_2 \leq 0.312 </math> and <math>0.084 \leq l_2 \leq 0.088</math>.<ref  name=Poulsen/>

For Earth's tides one can calculate the tilt factor as <math>1 + k - h</math> and the gravimetric factor as <math>1 + h - (3/2)k</math>, where subscript two is assumed.<ref name=Cartwright/>
